interest: This file offers an unusual perspective on individual expatriation and voluntary foreign military recruitment during the interwar period, capturing an American citizen's attempt to enlist in the Imperial Japanese Army in February 1933, precisely around the time of Japan's departure from the League of Nations over Manchuria. It illustrates how ordinary individuals, particularly former merchant seamen, navigated global mobility and perceived foreign military service as a transactional inducement for immigration and naturalization. Additionally, Dawson's ambivalent preference between becoming a naturalized subject in Japan or colonial French Indochina sheds light on idiosyncratic personal motivations during the Great Depression, while documenting how such unconventional inquiries were received and filed within the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.2221/1) consists of a two-page letter dated February 10, 1933, from Kenneth Dawson, an American-born resident of Miami, Florida, addressed to the Office of the Consul General in Washington, D.C. Dawson explains that having traveled around the world—including stops in Japan and French Indochina—he desires to renounce his American citizenship and become a naturalized citizen of either Japan or French Indochina. He reports that he has already contacted the French and Japanese embassies, having formally applied to the Japanese Consul General to enlist in the Japanese Army as an inducement for entry and naturalization, and he requests the State Department's cooperation to facilitate this transition, citing previous seaman passport records on file at the Customs House in Washington.

subfiles.about: An American citizen writes to the State Department seeking assistance and foreign consular cooperation to naturalize in Japan or French Indochina and enlist in the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Kenneth Dawson, an American citizen residing in Miami, Florida, writes to the Office of the Consul General in Washington requesting facilitation for his expatriation and naturalization in either Japan or French Indochina following a round-the-world journey. He notes that he has already submitted applications to the French and Japanese embassies in Washington, specifically requesting enlistment in the Japanese Army as an inducement to enter Japan and obtain citizenship. Dawson asks the State Department to assist and cooperate with foreign consuls to fulfill his request, providing details from a prior seaman's passport issued in Washington and referencing Columbus, Georgia.
